title: What Happens When Your Eyelid Won't Stop Twitching?
sources: Cleveland Clinic, 'Myokymia' (eyelid myokymia is a slow, uncontrollable twitching with wavelike contractions in the eyelids; 'You can have it in your upper or lower eyelids, but lower is more common'; 'happens because of malfunctions somewhere in your nervous system'; triggers: tiredness or sleep deprivation, caffeine, nicotine, dry eyes, fatigue, stress; 'extremely common and usually harmless'; 'Most cases go away within days or weeks without any treatment'; see a provider 'if eyelid myokymia doesn't go away after a few weeks', sooner if it spreads to other parts of your face; treatment may be an option if it happens consistently for at least three months): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/myokymia

Cleveland Clinic, 'Eye Twitching' (muscles in or near your eye move without you controlling them; myokymia twitches are most common in the eyelids, especially the lower ones; triggers include stress, not enough sleep, caffeine or nicotine, eye strain, fatigue; see an eye doctor if it affects your vision or worries you, right away for any vision change): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/17663-eye-twitching

American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki, 'Eyelid Myokymia' (asynchronous discharges within the orbicularis oculi muscle; 'Single motor units may fire several times per second at a frequency of 3-8 Hz'; typically one-sided and more common in the lower lid; usually benign and self-limited, resolving within minutes to weeks; triggers include stress, fatigue, caffeine, sleep deprivation, prolonged screen time): https://eyewiki.aao.org/Eyelid_Myokymia

Tease (next video): Yang W, Sahota R, Das S, 'Snap, crackle and pop: when sneezing leads to crackling in the neck', BMJ Case Reports 2018 (a 34-year-old man pinched his nose and closed his mouth to stop a forceful sneeze and tore the back of his throat; recovered fully), via ScienceDaily 2018-01-15: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2018/01/180115184339.htm

lines.text: What happens when your eyelid won't stop twitching?
Its muscle can fire up to eight times a second. Gone in weeks, or months?
lines.caps: ITS *MUSCLE | CAN *FIRE | UP TO *8 | TIMES A *SECOND | GONE IN *WEEKS | OR *MONTHS?

lines.text: Usually it's the lower lid, and the glitch is in your nerves.
Ever had it flicker through a whole video call?
Here's the twist: the trigger is usually your week.
Short sleep, extra coffee, stress, screens.
Weeks. Most fade on their own.
